opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think anyone has a clean answer yet, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who claims they do. A trillion tokens isn't just a bigger version of a million-token window. At that scale the problem changes character.

The naive picture is that you stretch the attention window further and further. That breaks down well before a trillion tokens, and not only because of compute cost. Even if you could afford full attention, the model wasn't trained to keep a coherent picture over that span. You see degradation: it attends to the wrong things, gets lost in the middle, and its reasoning quality drifts as the context fills with noise.

So I think stability at that scale comes from a few things working together.

First, the architecture has to stop treating every token as equally deserving of attention. Some form of sparse or hierarchical attention, or a learned compression of the past, is almost unavoidable. The model needs to decide what to keep in high resolution, what to summarize, and what it can retrieve later if needed. That's closer to how memory works than to how a context window works today.

Second, and I think this matters more than people realize, is training. You can't expect a model to use a huge context well if it has never been trained on tasks that require it. We need data and objectives where using information from very far back actually changes the outcome. A lot of long-context benchmarks today can be solved with shallow retrieval, needle-in-a-haystack style, and that doesn't teach the model to reason across the whole thing.

Third is the agentic angle. In practice, a trillion-token context probably won't be one giant prompt. It'll be a model living inside a long-running process, writing notes, organizing its own memory, revisiting things. Then stability is less about whether attention can span a trillion tokens and more about whether the model can manage its own state over time without accumulating errors. That's partly a capability question and partly a reinforcement learning question: you have to reward the model for keeping a consistent, accurate picture over long horizons.

If I had to bet, the breakthrough won't be a single trick. It'll be architecture, training data, and RL co-designed so the model actually learns to treat long context as working memory rather than a giant pile of text it happens to be able to see.

r001.rationale: The response mentions rewarding consistency over long horizons, but does not identify the time required to reward an entire one-trillion-token trajectory as a training bottleneck.

r002.rationale: The response argues that models need training on tasks requiring long-range context; it does not state that shorter post-training tasks can usually activate stable trillion-token capability in models pretrained at that length.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer in character as the guest, Fuli Luo, speaking directly to the host's question.

Honestly, I think "one trillion tokens of context" is a bit of a misleading framing if you take it literally. Nobody is going to put a trillion tokens into a single attention window and hope the model stays coherent. The real question is: how does a model keep stable behavior as the amount of information it has to reason over grows by orders of magnitude? And I think the answer is a combination of a few things, not one trick.

The first is that the model has to actually know how to use long context, not just tolerate it. There's a big gap between "the model doesn't crash at two million tokens" and "the model finds the right needle, synthesizes across the whole thing, and doesn't get distracted by irrelevant material." Most of that gap is a training problem, not an architecture problem. If your long-context data is just concatenated documents, the model learns to ignore most of the window, because most of it genuinely is noise. You have to construct training signals where the dependencies really do span the full length, where the answer at the end depends on something buried in the middle, where there are decoys. Otherwise the capability you measure on benchmarks is fake.

The second is memory and retrieval as a first-class part of the system. At very large scales, the model should be deciding what to keep in working memory and what to compress or store externally. A human reading a thousand-page document doesn't hold every sentence in mind. They build a summary, they keep pointers, they go back when they need to. I think the stable version of trillion-token capability looks more like that: a model with a learned sense of what matters, plus the ability to re-read. The attention mechanism itself can be sparse or hierarchical, but the important part is that the model is trained to manage its own memory rather than having us bolt on a retrieval system afterward and hope it cooperates.

The third thing, and people underestimate this, is consistency of the base model's behavior. Instability over long contexts often shows up as drift: the model slowly changes its style, forgets the instruction from the beginning, starts contradicting itself. That's partly a position problem, the model has seen very few examples at those positions during training, and partly an alignment problem, the model never had to maintain a commitment over that horizon. So you need RL or post-training signals that specifically reward holding a goal across very long trajectories. Agentic tasks are actually a natural source of this, because an agent working for hours generates exactly that kind of long, dependent sequence.

So my short answer would be: stable long-context capability is not something you get by making the window bigger. You get it by training the model on data where length actually matters, by giving it a learned way to manage memory instead of brute-force attention, and by post-training it to stay consistent over long horizons. If you do those three things, the number of tokens becomes much less scary. If you don't, a trillion-token context is mostly just a very expensive way to get confused.

astra-6.text:
I think we first have to distinguish between accepting a trillion tokens and actually using that context reliably. Those are very different capabilities. If a model can find one sentence in a huge input but cannot connect evidence across it, resolve contradictions, or recognize that some information is outdated, I wouldn’t call that stable capability.

My intuition is that simply extending the context window won’t be enough. We need a system that can organize information at multiple levels: keep detailed records, build useful summaries, and return to the original evidence when necessary. The difficult part is deciding what to preserve. Something that looks irrelevant now may become essential to a later question, so compression needs to be reversible through access to the source.

Training also has to reward that behavior. The model needs tasks where success depends on maintaining and updating information over long sequences, not just retrieving a few isolated facts. And evaluation should test whether its answers remain consistent as the context grows and new evidence arrives.

So I would frame this as a problem of memory, learning, and verification together. A trillion-token window is a capacity target. Stable capability means the model can reliably identify what matters, reason from it, and recognize when it hasn’t recovered enough evidence to answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to define what we mean by stable capability. Being able to accept a trillion tokens is one thing; being able to use the relevant information reliably is another. If the model can find a sentence but cannot connect it to evidence elsewhere in the context, we haven’t really solved the problem.

At that scale, I would think about memory as a hierarchy. Some information needs to remain available in its original form, some can be summarized, and some should be retrieved only when needed. The difficult part is deciding what to preserve. A detail that looks unimportant now could become essential to a question much later, so compression needs a path back to the original evidence.

Training also has to reward more than retrieval. We need tasks that require the model to combine distant information, handle contradictions, and update its conclusions when new evidence arrives. And we should test whether its answers remain consistent as we add irrelevant material or move the evidence around.

So I don’t think this will come simply from extending the context window. It requires the architecture, the training objective, and the memory mechanism to work together. The goal is reliable reasoning over that context, not just the ability to fit it in.
